text.p: Aircraft maker Boeing Co.'s stock dived Monday, but other blue chips reversed course and climbed, ending a three-session downward spiral.
The dollar closed higher in New York -- though off its best levels in Asian trading -- as Group of Seven finance ministers left room for the dollar to keep going up, currency traders said.
In the bond market, long-term interest rates edged lower.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 44.15 points to close at 6,783.02. In the broader market, advancing issues outnumbered declines 1,350 to 1,083 on moderate volume of about 402 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Boeing, one of 30 stocks in the Dow, slid $6.625 to $95.375 after reporting earnings that disappointed investors and warning that production of newer aircraft was likely to keep profit margins under pressure for the near-term.
But that apparently did not concern most investors.

"It appears no one chose to draw the inference Boeing's problems will translate into the same kinds of problems for other companies," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co. "That suggests there's still a high degree of confidence in this market."
Interest rate-sensitive stocks, which would suffer the most should inflation pick up, put in a strong performance.
The gains, concentrated in bank stocks, surprised some on Wall Street, coming as they did just ahead of an extremely heavy calendar of economic data.
Beyond the upturn in bank stocks, the broad market's performance was cautious and mixed ahead of key economic data.
Due early Tuesday is the first-quarter Employment Cost Index -- a closely watched barometer of wage inflation.
With employment, Gross Domestic Product and manufacturing numbers all due later in the week, analysts said the mood was likely to become even more cautious for the next few days.
"We still have a vary full plate in front of us," said Dick Stein, vice president at U.S. Clearing Corp. "This is a case where the other team has the ball and the rest of us play defence."

Bonds were mostly higher, with the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond rising 11/32, or $3.44 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 7.11 percent from Friday's close of 7.14 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

In currency markets, the dollar climbed to a 37-month peak against the German mark and near its 55-month high against the Japanese yen after the statement from Sunday's meeting of G7 officials in Washington was more lenient than traders had anticipated.

Traders said neither the official statement after the gathering nor comments by officials gave any hint they plan to step in to foreign exchange markets to curb the dollar's rise, a measure the United States has not taken since August 1995.

The dollar stood at 1.7325 German marks in late New York trading, below its high of 1.7389 but above 1.7275 late in New York on Friday. The dollar rose to 126.89 yen, below its high for the day of 127.08, but above 126.25 at Friday's close.
Wheat prices fell sharply after rains fell in parched areas of the European wheat belt, easing worries about the threat of drought.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for May delivery closed 11-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $4.12. At the Kansas City Board of Trade, hard red winter wheat for May delivery ended down a sharp 21 cents at $4.49 a bushel.
Overseas, the London Stock Exchange's FTSE 100 index closed 20 points, or 0.46 percent, higher at 4,389.7. Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average ended up 57.51 points, or 0.31 percent, at 18,670.37.
